opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think my view on it has evolved a bit over time.

For a lot of the locomotion work we've done, we deliberately avoided demonstrations. The idea was to see how far pure reinforcement learning in simulation can go: you define a reward, run thousands of robots in parallel on a GPU, and let the policy discover how to walk on its own. For locomotion that works surprisingly well, because the task is fairly well defined and you can shape the reward to get good behavior without anyone telling the robot what the motion should look like.

The limitation shows up when you care not just about *whether* the robot solves the task but *how* it solves it. RL is very good at exploiting whatever you give it. If your reward has a loophole, the policy will find it, and you get gaits that are technically fine but look strange, or are hard on the hardware. Then you end up spending a lot of time tuning reward terms, which is a kind of hidden manual engineering.

That's where demonstrations become really useful. They help in a few ways.

First, they can define the style of the motion. Instead of hand-crafting a dozen reward terms for foot clearance, joint smoothness and so on, you give the policy reference motions, from motion capture of animals or humans or from an existing controller, and reward it for staying close to that distribution. Adversarial motion priors are a nice example. The RL still handles robustness and recovery, but the demonstrations anchor what "natural" looks like.

Second, they help with exploration. For harder, longer-horizon tasks, like manipulation or complex parkour-style behaviors, the reward can be very sparse, and random exploration may never stumble onto the solution. A few demonstrations put the policy in the right region of the solution space, and RL can then refine and robustify from there.

Third, there's the combination with imitation learning at scale. Pure imitation tends to be brittle. It only knows the states it has seen, and small errors compound. RL is good at filling that gap: you practice in simulation, you see failures and recover from them. So I see the two as complementary. Demonstrations tell you what to do, and RL teaches you how to do it reliably under disturbances and in situations the demonstrator never covered.

The open challenge is getting demonstrations that actually match the robot. A human's body isn't a quadruped's or even a humanoid's, so there's always a retargeting problem, and if you follow the demonstration too closely you can force the robot into motions that aren't physically feasible for it. The art is finding the right balance: use demonstrations as a strong prior, but leave RL enough freedom to adapt them to the robot's own dynamics.

r001.rationale: The response says a few demonstrations can put a policy in the right region for exploration, but it does not clearly connect that exploration guidance to information extracted from human demonstrations; human motion capture is mentioned separately as a source of reference motions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that for a long time, at least in the legged locomotion world, we kind of didn't need demonstrations. You could just write a reward function, throw it in a massively parallel simulator, and the robot would figure out how to walk. And that worked really well, but it also hid a problem. The moment you move to harder tasks, like parkour, or very dynamic motions, or anything where the robot has to do something that isn't an obvious consequence of "move forward and don't fall," the exploration problem becomes really brutal. You have this huge space of possible behaviors, the reward is sparse or delayed, and pure RL just spends an enormous amount of time flailing around before it stumbles on anything useful.

So the way I see demonstrations is really as a way of shaping the exploration. They don't have to be perfect, and they definitely don't need to be from the same embodiment. If you take, say, motion capture data from a human, or a trajectory from an animal, or even a rough hand-designed motion, that gives the policy a prior about what region of behavior space is worth looking at. And then RL does what it's actually good at, which is refining that in the real dynamics of the robot, dealing with contact, dealing with the fact that the robot has different mass and different actuators than whatever produced the demonstration.

The other thing that's underappreciated is that demonstrations are a much more natural way to specify what you want than a reward function. If I want a robot to do a backflip or a specific dance move, writing that as a weighted sum of reward terms is really painful, and you end up with reward hacking where the robot finds some weird behavior that technically scores well. Showing it a reference motion and saying "be close to this" is a far more intuitive interface. So I think of it as two things at once: a prior that makes the optimization tractable, and a specification language that's easier for humans to work with.

Where I'd push back a bit is on the idea that you should just imitate. If you treat the demonstration as ground truth and only do behavior cloning, you inherit all the mistakes in the data, and you can't exceed it. The interesting regime is where imitation gets you into the right neighborhood and then the task reward and the simulation let the policy go beyond what was demonstrated, because it has to be robust to perturbations, to terrain, to things the demonstrator never encountered. That combination is, I think, where most of the exciting results are going to come from in the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations can shape exploration by giving the policy a prior about useful behaviors, and mentions human motion capture. It does not communicate that limited information extracted from those demonstrations guides exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think demonstrations are a very useful way to give reinforcement learning a starting point. If you ask a robot to learn a complex task from scratch, it might spend a lot of time exploring without ever finding a behavior that succeeds. A demonstration can show it roughly what it should be doing, so it doesn’t have to discover everything by trial and error.

But I wouldn’t necessarily want the robot to just copy the demonstration exactly. You want it to adapt to its own dynamics and to situations that weren’t in the demonstration. So you can use demonstrations to guide the learning, and then use reinforcement learning to improve the behavior and make it more robust. They’re complementary: demonstrations help with exploration, and reinforcement learning gives you a way to go beyond what was demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations can guide exploration and reinforce learning, but it does not explain that the robot uses limited information extracted from human demonstrations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think demonstrations are a very useful way to guide exploration. If you start reinforcement learning from scratch, the robot has to discover both what the task is and how to solve it through trial and error. For a complicated task, it might never encounter a successful behavior, so it never gets a useful learning signal.

A demonstration gives you a starting point. You can use it to initialize a policy, or to guide the reward toward behaviors that look like the demonstration, and then let reinforcement learning improve from there. The robot doesn’t necessarily have to copy the motion exactly—it needs to adapt it to its own dynamics and recover when things go differently. So I see demonstrations as providing that initial direction, with reinforcement learning making the behavior robust.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations can guide exploration by providing a starting point, but it does not communicate that only limited information is extracted from human demonstrations.
